label: Camera angle
description: Camera height, viewing direction, overhead viewpoints, tilted angles, and subjective viewpoints such as over the shoulder or through a participant's eyes.
notes: Camera height, viewing direction, camera roll and subjective viewpoints belong here, phrased as short viewpoint names. Top-down and bird’s-eye view share one entry; overhead flat lay specifically means objects arranged on a flat surface, while the aerial drone view looks obliquely across a larger setting. The over-the-shoulder shot needs two people (its people tag) and is opt-in, drawn only when asked for; the point-of-view shot looks through a participant's eyes. camera.shot_size owns framing distance and camera.selfie owns selfies. camera.lens owns lenses, and camera.film_look owns film and format looks. Directions describe the camera relative to the subject, not the direction of lighting.

values.look: The camera sits at the subject’s eye height, looking straight across without looking up or down.
The camera looks horizontally from chest height, with a standing person’s head above the camera’s center line.
The camera looks horizontally from the hips, placing nearby waists at its height and heads well above it.
The camera tilts upward from below the subject, showing undersides and making the subject rise above the viewer.
The camera looks across the scene from the floor or ground, with the nearest surface prominent in the foreground.
The camera is positioned at knee height, placing lower legs close to its center and the upper body above.
From almost on the ground, the camera points steeply upward beneath the subject toward the sky or ceiling.
The camera looks down diagonally, revealing the tops of heads and objects along with the floor or ground.
The camera points straight down onto the scene, showing top surfaces and positions across the ground below.
Objects lie arranged on one flat surface, photographed directly from above with no horizon visible.
An elevated, oblique view spans rooftops or landscape, showing both top surfaces and distant terrain.
The camera rolls sideways so the horizon slopes and upright objects lean diagonally across the frame.
The subject faces the camera squarely, with its front visible and both sides appearing roughly symmetrical.
The camera sees the front and one side together; on a face, both eyes show but one side appears narrower.
The camera sees the subject directly from one side; on a face, one eye shows and the nose projects in silhouette.
The camera sees the back and one side together, with little or none of the subject’s front visible.
The camera faces the subject’s back directly; a person’s face is hidden and the back of the head is visible.
The back of one person’s head and shoulder edges the foreground while another person faces them beyond.
The scene appears through a participant’s eyes, often with their hands or feet entering the bottom of the frame.
